content: Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of illnesses caused by several distinct families of viruses. These diseases affect multiple organ systems in the body, damage the cardiovascular system, and impair the body’s ability to function independently. In addition to VHFs, other serious infectious diseases, such as Nipah and Hendra viruses, also require specialized laboratory handling due to their high pathogenicity and the lack of effective vaccines or treatments. VHFs, as well as Nipah and Hendra diseases, can range in severity from mild illness to life-threatening conditions. Symptoms may include bleeding or hemorrhaging. The geographic distribution of these viruses is determined by the habitats of the animals that naturally carry them. Arenaviruses Arenaviruses are associated with specific rodent species that act as reservoirs, meaning the rodents carry the virus without becoming ill. Humans can become infected through contact with the urine, droppings, or nesting materials of infected rodents, inhalation of contaminated air, bites or scratches from infected rodents, consumption of food contaminated by rodent excretions, or contact with infected individuals in the case of certain arenaviruses (e.g., Chapare, Lassa, Machupo, and Lujo viruses). Bunyavirales Order Viruses in the Bunyavirales order are transmitted by rodents or insects such as mosquitoes, ticks, or sand flies. These viruses can cause diseases ranging from mild to severe in both humans and animals. While many of these viruses do not spread between humans, person-to-person transmission of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever has been documented in healthcare settings with inadequate infection control measures. Filoviruses Filoviruses, such as Ebola and Marburg viruses, cause severe illness in humans and nonhuman primates. The Egyptian rousette bat (_Rousettus aegyptiacus_) is the natural reservoir for the Marburg virus, although infected bats do not exhibit symptoms. The natural reservoir for ebolaviruses remains unknown, but bats are suspected to play a role. Once introduced into human populations, filoviruses can spread through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected individuals. Healthcare workers and caregivers without proper personal protective equipment (PPE) are at increased risk of infection. Flaviviruses Flaviviruses are distributed worldwide and are primarily transmitted by mosquitoes and ticks. These viruses can cause diseases ranging from mild to severe, including death. They also affect animals, leading to significant economic and social consequences in affected regions. Paramyxoviruses Paramyxoviruses are known to cause sudden respiratory illnesses. Among the viruses in the _Paramyxoviridae_ family, Hendra and Nipah viruses are particularly concerning due to their ability to cause severe disease, their potential for animal-to-human and human-to-human transmission, and the absence of available vaccines or treatments. These viruses require handling in specialized biosafety level 4 laboratories. Prevention Preventing VHFs and other high-consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) depends on understanding the host reservoir and modes of transmission. Preventive measures include using insect repellents, bed nets, and protective clothing, as well as implementing disinfection protocols when caring for infected individuals. In cases of rodent infestations, sealing entry points and setting traps in homes and buildings are recommended.
